problem: Floor-plan-guided monocular navigation (FloNa) encodes the floor plan as a plain image and fuses it with RGB via a shared transformer encoder, giving a superficial fusion that wastes the plan's explicit connectivity. It also needs huge training data and is fragile to localization error.
motivation: Floor plans are stable global priors that remove the need for exploration or mapping, but the modal gap between egocentric RGB and top-down plans, and missing furniture in plans, make fusion hard. Explicitly separating global directional guidance (from plan topology) from local geometry (from depth) should give efficient and collision-safe navigation with far less data.
key_idea: Condition a diffusion policy on two complementary cues: a global A* shortest-path waypoint sequence from the floor plan (directional cue) and monocular-RGB-derived depth features (local depth cue).
insight: Ablations show both cues matter: removing the explicit path (goal point only) causes the largest drop (SR 79.6→44.6 at τc=10), while replacing depth with RGB features drops SR to 64.2, so explicit floor-plan planning is more valuable than local depth. Training-time noise on path and pose gives robustness to noisy VO/F3Loc localization and yields better results than FloNa's Loc-FloDiff with ~150x less data (1.2M vs 180M samples).
method: Depth Cue Module: a pretrained diffusion-based monocular depth encoder (Marigold-style, Ke et al.) processes the current and past 4 RGB frames, followed by multi-head attention and averaging into a depth context; this is concatenated with the floor plan feature (EfficientNet-B0 + MLP) and the pose, and passed through an MLP to give the local cue C_l.

Localization Module: pose on the floor plan comes from GT (training), visual odometry (pySLAM), or F3Loc floor-plan localization at test time; pixel-to-world conversion uses the plan resolution and offset.

Directional Cue Module: A* computes the shortest path on the floor plan from the current position to the goal, converts it to metric and then agent-frame coordinates, and keeps the first m points (~1.2 m) as global path guidance C_g.

Diffusion Policy: a DDPM with a conditional 1D-conv UNet (3 down, bottleneck, 2 up) predicts m×2 future waypoints (each about 4 cm); C_l is injected in every module and C_g through residual blocks into the first down and second up modules; loss is MSE on the noise; square-cosine schedule.

Noise-perturbation training: uniform noise on the shortest path with an upper bound growing as α·sin(iπ/2N) (α=0.1), and Gaussian noise on the GT position (σ 0.1) and orientation (π/36), for robustness to VO/F3Loc errors.
Training: 1.2M samples from FloNa's Gibson data (67 scenes, 20,214 episodes), one sample every 5 frames with the goal set as the episode's final waypoint; 20 epochs on 8×4090.

setting.backbone: Diffusion policy (conditional 1D UNet, DDPM) with a pretrained diffusion-based depth encoder (Marigold-style), EfficientNet-B0 floor plan encoder and multi-head attention, trained on FloNa data
setting.training_data: FloNa dataset: 67 Gibson scenes, 20,214 episodes, subsampled to 1.2M samples (vs 180M for Loc-FloDiff)
setting.observation: monocular RGB (5-frame history) + floor plan image + pose estimate (GT / VO / F3Loc)
setting.action_space: predicted 2D waypoint sequences (m=32 steps, ~4 cm each) converted to velocities by a PD controller
setting.simulator: Habitat-style Gibson simulator; test on Gibson and HM3D scenes
setting.privileged: GT pose for the (GT) variants; floor plan of the environment given; VO/F3Loc variants use estimated pose only

numbers_note: The paper's own table label is 'GlocDiff'/model macro; the FloNa benchmark is not in the canonical list, so 'other:' names are used. Values shown are for τc=∞ with a few other τc values in eval_set_note; the full tables also give τc=10/30/50. Real robot: 40% SR on 10 episodes (3 trials each, τc=0, τd=20 cm).
results: With GT pose, the method reaches SR 97.6/SPL 72.36 on Gibson and SR 91.8/SPL 71.69 on HM3D (τc=∞), clearly above Loc-FloDiff (GT) at 66.0/48.2 and 53.2/40.41, despite 1.2M vs 180M training samples. It degrades more gracefully than Loc-FloDiff with F3Loc pose, and VO gives better results than F3Loc. On a real AGV it achieved 40% SR without fine-tuning.
limitations: Real-world success rate is only 40% on 10 episodes with a strict zero-collision requirement, and it relies on LiDAR odometry with a pre-calibrated initial pose.
Performance still depends heavily on localization quality: with VO/F3Loc pose SR falls significantly, especially under strict collision limits.
Inference speed is only ~1.21 Hz on the Jetson AGX Orin; the evaluation covers only Gibson and HM3D with a custom collision-thresholded protocol.
